opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that a lot of it was luck, plus a kind of stubbornness that happened to fit well with how research mathematics works.

When I was an undergrad I didn't feel like a prodigy. There were people around me who were much faster, who had done olympiads since they were very young and could see a solution almost instantly. What I had was a willingness to sit with a problem for a very long time and not get bored. Research rewards that. You aren't solving a competition problem in four and a half hours. You might be stuck on one lemma for weeks, and the people who succeed are often the ones who keep coming back to it.

I was also very fortunate with mentors. Professors gave me problems that were the right size: hard enough to be real research, but not so hard that an undergraduate had no chance. That's a skill on their part, and people don't talk about it enough. When a professor recognizes a student's work, part of what they're recognizing is that the student took a well-chosen problem seriously and pushed it to the end.

So I try not to read too much into the recognition as a statement about talent. I read it more as encouragement, a signal that I was doing the right kind of work and should keep going. And it changed how I saw myself. Before that I thought of math as something I was good at in school. After that I started to think of it as something I could actually contribute to, where I could produce something new that didn't exist before.

The other thing I'd say is that recognition can be a trap if you aren't careful. Once people praise you, you can start optimizing for the next prize or the next letter, and that's not the same as optimizing for interesting mathematics. I've tried to remember that what I actually loved was the feeling of finally understanding why something is true. That feeling is the real reward, and it's also what later pulled me toward questions about how machines might reason mathematically.

r001.rationale: She describes the recognition as “encouragement” and a signal that she “should keep going.”

fable-5.1.text:
I think the recognition mattered less for what it said about me and more for what it taught me about how mathematics actually works as a community. When I was an undergraduate, I was working on problems in number theory and combinatorics, and honestly a lot of the time I had no idea whether what I was doing was good. You sit alone with a problem for months, you make a little progress, you get stuck, and there's no external signal telling you whether you're on the right track.

So when professors took my work seriously, the first thing I felt wasn't pride, it was relief. It was confirmation that the thing I'd been obsessing over was a real thing that other people cared about. And the second thing I felt was that I owed something back. Because in mathematics, recognition from a senior person isn't really a prize. It's an invitation. They're saying, "Come in, you can sit at this table, now show us what else you can do."

I also try to be honest with myself about how much of it was luck. I had advisors who were generous with their time, I happened to pick problems that connected to things people were actively thinking about, and I was at institutions with a lot of resources. There were people around me who were just as capable and didn't get the same visibility, sometimes simply because they were working on something less fashionable or didn't have the right mentor at the right moment.

So I hold it loosely. The awards and the recognition opened doors, and I'm grateful for that. But the part I actually value is the taste I developed, learning what a good problem looks like, learning when to push and when to let go. That's what carried over when I later moved into AI and building things. The prizes stay on a shelf. The way of thinking comes with you.

r001.rationale: She describes the recognition as an invitation to join the mathematical community and continue demonstrating what she can do, suggesting encouragement to keep doing mathematics.

astra-6.text: I think of it as encouragement to keep exploring. When a professor takes your work seriously, it can help you develop confidence in your own questions, even while you’re still learning how to approach them. I wouldn’t interpret that recognition as meaning I’d already proved myself as a mathematician. I’d see it as a reason to keep working, stay curious, and learn from people who can challenge my thinking.
